response:
The question of whether Atlanta's late-2000s test-score surge was real first entered public view through journalism rather than through any official audit. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution published analyses showing statistically improbable score gains at Atlanta schools, and that reporting led to the suspicious gains appearing on Georgia's Criterion-Referenced Competency Tests. The CRCT was the state's high-stakes accountability instrument. Its results determined whether schools met federal benchmarks and whether administrators earned bonuses, which is why sharp year-over-year jumps in individual buildings attracted scrutiny from statisticians and reporters alike.

Investigators had to weigh two explanations for those jumps, and the evidence never required choosing only one. At least one of the following held, perhaps both: some of the Atlanta score gains resulted from educators altering student answer sheets, or some of the Atlanta score gains resulted from genuine instructional improvement. To separate the two, the Georgia Governor's Office of Student Achievement commissioned an erasure analysis of the 2009 answer sheets. The method relied on optical scanners that detect residual graphite where a bubble has been changed. The erasure analysis counted wrong-to-right erasures on student answer sheets, and it took that form because many Atlanta classrooms showed wrong-to-right erasure rates far above the state average. That erasure pattern indicates the tampering with answer sheets described above. Children revising their own work produce erasures in all directions and at modest rates. Clusters of corrections that turn wrong answers into right ones, concentrated in particular classrooms, point instead to adults changing responses after testing. The pattern held even though genuine instructional progress was present in parts of the district.

Statistical anomalies alone could not establish intent or identify who had changed the answers, so the inquiry moved to sworn testimony and document review. The Federal Bureau of Investigation led the inquiry into the Atlanta test scores. Governor Sonny Perdue appointed special investigators to examine the Atlanta schools. The special investigators' report was released in July 2011. In other words, in July 2011 the findings of the governor's special investigation were made public. The investigative team, which included former state attorney general Mike Bowers, interviewed teachers, principals, and central-office staff. They obtained confessions from educators who described erasure sessions held behind closed doors, and they found records showing that warnings about irregularities had been ignored or suppressed.

The scale of the misconduct was the central question the report answered. The investigators found evidence of cheating at only 12 Atlanta schools. By contrast, the special investigators concluded that systematic cheating had occurred in 44 of the 56 schools they examined. That conclusion settles the tension between the genuine instructional gains and the anomalous erasure rates. Real improvement may have occurred in some classrooms, but tampering pervaded so many schools that the district's celebrated trajectory could no longer be read as evidence of instructional success. The report also described a culture of fear in which teachers who missed targets faced public humiliation or dismissal, which explains why misconduct spread across buildings rather than remaining isolated.

The criminal phase followed. A Fulton County grand jury in 2013 indicted former superintendent Beverly Hall and thirty-four other educators under Georgia's racketeering statute. Prosecutors argued that the district had operated as a corrupt enterprise whose output was falsified data. Many defendants accepted plea agreements, and a jury in 2015 convicted eleven of those who went to trial. The disposition of the case against Hall herself admits of exactly two outcomes, and one of them must be the case: either Beverly Hall stood trial on the racketeering charges, or Beverly Hall never stood trial on the racketeering charges. The two cannot both be true. The Fulton County Superior Court settled the question when it postponed Hall's trial because of her advanced cancer, and after her death in March 2015 the case against her closed without a trial. Taken together, the erasure statistics, the governor's investigation, and the prosecutions show how investigators turned a statistical suspicion into a documented account of systematic answer-sheet tampering.
